items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with dry, intensely itchy, excoriated erythematous plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae for six months. In accordance with NICE guideline CG57, what is the mandatory foundational therapy for all severity levels of atopic eczema?
o: Liberal, frequent application of leave-on emollients
Potent topical corticosteroid applied continuously for 6 months
items.exp: NICE guideline CG57 emphasizes that liberal and frequent application of leave-on emollients (in quantities of 250-500 g per week for a child) forms the essential foundation of eczema care across all severity tiers, even when the skin appears clear.
r: Correct: Liberal emollients are the mandatory foundation across all eczema severities.
Oral systemic steroids are reserved for severe crisis flares under specialist care, never routine baseline.
Continuous potent topical steroids cause severe skin atrophy, striae and adrenal suppression.
Continuous prophylactic antibiotics drive bacterial resistance without improving barrier function.
items.kp: Liberal, frequent leave-on emollients form the mandatory foundation of atopic eczema management.
items.source: NICE guideline CG57: Atopic eczema in under 12s

x.key: Liberal frequent emollients are the essential foundation of atopic eczema care.

others.B: Oral steroids are not routine baseline.
others.C: Continuous potent steroids cause cutaneous atrophy.

x.pearl: Emollients should always be smoothed gently onto the skin in the downward direction of hair growth to prevent folliculitis.
x.clues: Child, flexural dry itchy plaques, mandatory foundational treatment.
x.ddx: Seborrheic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, scabies, psoriasis.
x.mech: Replenishing lipid bilayers restores defective stratum corneum hydration and reduces transepidermal water loss.
x.lo: State the foundational role of emollients in atopic eczema management.
x.rev: Liberal emollients form the mandatory foundation of atopic eczema therapy.

items.q: A 6-year-old girl with atopic eczema has an acute inflammatory flare affecting her cheeks and eyelids with erythema and excoriation. What potency of topical corticosteroid is recommended for her facial skin?
o: Topical corticosteroids are strictly contraindicated on the face
items.exp: NICE CG57 recommends matching topical corticosteroid potency to anatomical site and severity. The face and flexures have thin stratum corneum and are highly vulnerable to dermal atrophy, telangiectasia and perioral dermatitis; only mild-potency corticosteroids (such as 1% hydrocortisone) should be used on the face, for short courses of 3-5 days.
r: Correct: Mild-potency steroids (hydrocortisone 1%) are recommended for facial eczema.
Very potent steroids on the face cause rapid, severe dermal atrophy, striae and perioral dermatitis.
Potent steroids are inappropriate for delicate facial skin in children.
Topical steroids can be used safely on the face when appropriately matched to mild potency.
items.kp: Only mild-potency corticosteroids (e.g. hydrocortisone 1%) should be used on the face in atopic eczema.
items.source: NICE guideline CG57: Atopic eczema in under 12s

x.key: Mild-potency corticosteroids are indicated for facial eczema to avoid atrophy.

others.B: Very potent steroids cause severe facial skin thinning.
others.C: Potent steroids are too strong for facial skin.
others.D: Mild steroids are safe for short courses.

x.pearl: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g. tacrolimus 0.03%) are licensed second-line alternatives for facial eczema that avoid atrophy.
x.clues: Child, acute eczema flare on cheeks and eyelids, appropriate steroid potency.
x.ddx: Seborrheic dermatitis, perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis.
x.mech: Thin facial epidermis absorbs glucocorticoids avidly; mild potency limits suppression of dermal fibroblast collagen synthesis.
x.lo: Select the appropriate potency of topical corticosteroid for facial eczema.
x.rev: Use mild-potency corticosteroids for facial atopic eczema to avoid dermal atrophy.

items.q: A 28-year-old hairdresser presents with dry, cracked, erythematous, painful fissures on her hands, predominantly on the dorsum of her hands and web spaces. Her symptoms worsen following long shifts with frequent shampooing and wet work, and improve during two-week holidays. Patch testing is negative. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Irritant contact dermatitis is a non-immunological physical and chemical disruption of the epidermal barrier caused by cumulative exposure to water, detergents, and chemicals in occupational wet work (hairdressers, healthcare workers, cleaners). Patch testing is characteristically negative.
r: Correct: Negative patch testing and wet-work association define irritant contact dermatitis.
Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV immunological reaction that produces positive patch testing.
Tinea manuum typically presents as unilateral scaling with an active fungal border.
Psoriasis features thick well-demarcated silvery scaly plaques and nail pitting.
items.kp: Irritant contact dermatitis results from cumulative chemical/wet-work barrier damage and has negative patch tests.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines for the management of hand dermatitis

x.key: Negative patch tests and wet-work link indicate irritant contact dermatitis.

others.B: Allergic contact dermatitis has positive patch testing.
others.C: Tinea manuum is fungal and usually unilateral.
others.D: Psoriasis features silvery plaques and nail pits.

x.pearl: Irritant contact dermatitis accounts for approximately 80% of all occupational contact dermatitis cases.
x.clues: Hairdresser, wet work, dorsal hand fissures, negative patch test, holiday improvement.
x.ddx: Allergic contact dermatitis, pompholyx eczema, hand psoriasis, tinea manuum.
x.mech: Surfactants and repeated water immersion strip epidermal lipids, denature keratin, and trigger non-specific cytokine release.
x.lo: Differentiate irritant from allergic contact dermatitis.
x.rev: Irritant contact dermatitis is a non-allergic barrier disruption caused by wet work with negative patch testing.

items.q: A 22-year-old woman develops an intensely itchy, vesicular erythematous rash on her peri-umbilical abdomen directly beneath the metal stud of her new jeans, and on her earlobes beneath costume earrings. What is the immunological mechanism of this condition?
o: Type IV (delayed-type) cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to nickel
items.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (most commonly to nickel in costume jewellery and metal clothing studs) is a classical Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction mediated by hapten-specific sensitized CD4+ and CD8+ memory T-cells, manifesting 24-72 hours after antigen re-exposure.
r: Correct: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
Type I hypersensitivity is immediate, IgE-mediated (urticaria and anaphylaxis).
Type II is antibody-mediated cytotoxic (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Goodpasture).
Type III is immune-complex mediated (serum sickness, SLE, post-streptococcal GN).
items.kp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines on contact dermatitis

x.key: Allergic contact dermatitis is Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
x.pearl: Diagnostic confirmation is achieved via epicutaneous patch testing read at 48 and 72-96 hours.
x.clues: Rash under metal jeans stud and costume earrings, itchy, vesicular.
x.ddx: Irritant dermatitis, atopic eczema, fixed drug eruption.
x.mech: Nickel haptens penetrate the epidermis, bind HLA Class II on Langerhans cells, and prime effector memory T-lymphocytes.
x.lo: Identify the immunological mechanism of allergic contact dermatitis.
x.rev: Allergic contact dermatitis is mediated by Type IV delayed hypersensitivity.

next.text: Review patch testing and contact allergens.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic bilateral varicose veins presents with brownish hyperpigmentation, scaling, and pruritus around her lower medial ankles. Palpation reveals induration and inverted 'champagne bottle' tapering of the lower calves. Her Doppler ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is 1.0. What is the definitive physical treatment?
o: Continuous oral antibiotic therapy for 3 months
Immediate surgical debridement of intact skin
Complete bed rest with absolute leg immobilization
items.exp: Venous stasis eczema and lipodermatosclerosis result from chronic ambulatory venous hypertension. Graduated compression therapy (compression hosiery or bandages) reverses venous hypertension and accelerates healing, provided significant peripheral arterial disease has been excluded by an ABPI >0.8.
r: Correct: Graduated compression hosiery is definitive treatment once ABPI >0.8 confirms arterial patency.
Antibiotics have no role in uninfected venous eczema and haemosiderin staining.
Surgical debridement is contraindicated in non-ulcerated lipodermatosclerosis and causes chronic wounds.
Immobilization worsens venous pooling and increases deep vein thrombosis risk.
items.kp: Graduated compression therapy is definitive for venous stasis eczema once ABPI excludes arterial disease.
items.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Stasis eczema

x.key: Graduated compression therapy is definitive for venous eczema when ABPI >0.8.

others.C: Debridement of intact skin creates ulcers.

x.pearl: Brown pigmentation in venous stasis results from extravasated red blood cells breaking down into dermal haemosiderin.
x.clues: Varicose veins, ankle hyperpigmentation, champagne bottle leg, normal ABPI.
x.ddx: Cellulitis, contact dermatitis to ulcer dressings, necrobiosis lipoidica, morphoea.
x.mech: Valvular incompetence drives venous hypertension, capillary distension, fibrin cuffing, and extravasation of erythrocytes into dermis.
x.lo: Select the definitive therapy for venous stasis eczema.
x.rev: Graduated compression hosiery is the definitive treatment for venous stasis eczema once ABPI is normal.

next.text: Review NICE CKS on stasis eczema and compression.

items.q: A 25-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic, deep-seated 'tapioca pudding-like' vesicles along the lateral margins of his fingers and palms. The vesicles do not easily rupture and resolve with desquamation. What form of eczema is this?
items.exp: Pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema / vesicular hand dermatitis) is an acute or recurrent form of eczema characterized by intensely itchy, deep-seated, tapioca-like vesicles predominantly on the lateral borders of the fingers, palms, and soles.
r: Correct: Deep-seated pruritic vesicles on the lateral borders of the fingers represent pompholyx.
Nummular eczema forms circular, coin-shaped plaques on the limbs.
Asteatotic eczema presents with fine 'crazy paving' fissuring on dry shins in the elderly.
Herpetic whitlow causes localized grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base on a single digit.
items.kp: Pompholyx eczema presents with intensely pruritic deep-seated 'tapioca-like' vesicles on finger margins.
items.source: British Association of Dermatologists: Guidelines on hand dermatitis

x.key: Deep-seated tapioca-like vesicles on finger margins define pompholyx.

others.C: Asteatotic eczema is crazy-paving dry skin.

x.pearl: High-potency topical corticosteroids under occlusion or short courses of systemic steroids are used for severe acute flares.
x.clues: Young adult, intense itch, tapioca pudding-like vesicles, lateral finger margins.
x.ddx: Allergic contact dermatitis, tinea manuum, bullous impetigo, scabies.
x.mech: Intense spongiosis in the thick palmar epidermis forms tense intraepidermal vesicles rather than superficial pustules.
x.lo: Recognise the clinical morphology of pompholyx hand eczema.
x.rev: Pompholyx features deep-seated, intensely pruritic vesicles on lateral fingers and palms.

items.q: A 78-year-old man admitted to a geriatric ward during winter complains of severe itching and soreness on his lower legs. Examination of the anterior shins reveals dry, polygonal epidermal plates separated by fine red fissures resembling cracked porcelain or 'crazy paving'. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Asteatotic eczema (eczema craquelé) is caused by severe cutaneous lipid depletion and dehydration, common in elderly individuals exposed to low ambient humidity, frequent hot bathing and diuretics. It classically affects the shins, producing fine erythematous cracks in a 'crazy paving' or 'riverbed' pattern.
r: Correct: Dry cracked porcelain 'crazy paving' appearance on elderly shins is asteatotic eczema.
Stasis dermatitis features haemosiderin pigmentation and chronic venous signs.
Pre-tibial myxoedema causes non-pitting waxy peau d'orange plaques in Graves disease.
Ichthyosis vulgaris is an inherited lifelong scaling condition presenting in early childhood.
items.kp: Asteatotic eczema presents with a 'crazy paving' cracked porcelain appearance on dry shins in the elderly.
items.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Eczema - asteatotic

x.key: Crazy paving appearance on dry shins defines asteatotic eczema.

others.C: Pre-tibial myxoedema is linked to thyroid disease.

x.pearl: Treatment requires greasy ointment emollients, avoiding soap and hot baths, and short-term mild topical corticosteroids.
x.clues: Elderly male, winter, shins, fine red fissures, crazy paving pattern.
x.ddx: Cellulitis, venous eczema, xerosis cutis, allergic contact dermatitis.
x.mech: Age-related sebaceous and sweat gland atrophy leads to critical loss of intercellular lipid matrix and stratum corneum shrinkage.
x.lo: Recognise asteatotic eczema and its characteristic crazy-paving appearance.
x.rev: Asteatotic eczema causes a crazy-paving cracked appearance on dry elderly shins.

next.text: Review NICE CKS on asteatotic eczema.

items.q: A 45-year-old man presents with discrete, intensely itchy, coin-shaped erythematous scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of his arms and legs. There is no central clearing. Skin scrapings are negative for fungal hyphae. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Discoid (nummular) eczema is characterized by discrete, coin-shaped (discoid) erythematous, pruritic plaques without central clearing, commonly distributed on the limbs. In contrast to tinea corporis, it lacks an active advancing fungal edge and scrapings are negative.
r: Correct: Discrete coin-shaped itchy plaques without central clearing represent discoid eczema.
Tinea corporis displays central clearing with an active scaly border and positive fungal hyphae.
Plaque psoriasis features silvery-white scale, Auspitz sign and extensor predilection without coin-shaped exudation.
Bowen disease produces a single, slowly enlarging solitary plaque, not multiple bilateral lesions.
items.kp: Discoid eczema presents with discrete, intensely itchy, coin-shaped plaques without central clearing.
items.source: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: Eczema - discoid

x.key: Coin-shaped pruritic plaques without central clearing indicate discoid eczema.
x.pearl: Discoid eczema frequently requires potent topical corticosteroids combined with intensive emollient therapy.
x.clues: Coin-shaped itchy plaques on limbs, no central clearing, negative fungal scrapings.
x.ddx: Tinea corporis, plaque psoriasis, contact dermatitis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
x.mech: Intense epidermal spongiosis and dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltration localized in discrete rounded foci.
x.lo: Differentiate discoid eczema from tinea corporis.
x.rev: Discoid eczema presents with coin-shaped itchy plaques without central clearing.

next.text: Review NICE CKS on discoid eczema.

items.q: A child with atopic eczema has developed localized honey-coloured, golden crusting and weeping overlying excoriated eczema patches on his chin. Swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. What is the diagnosis and recommended management?
o: Secondary bacterial impetiginisation; treat with oral flucloxacillin (or topical fusidic acid for mild localized lesion)
Eczema herpeticum; treat with IV aciclovir
Fungal superinfection; treat with oral terbinafine
Normal eczema; continue emollients alone without antibiotics
items.exp: Secondary bacterial infection of eczema (impetiginisation) is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, presenting with weeping, pustules and honey-coloured golden crusts. NICE guidelines recommend oral flucloxacillin for widespread or systemic infection, or short-course topical fusidic acid for localized mild crusting, alongside continued emollients and topical steroids once infection is treated.
r: Correct: Honey-coloured crusts indicate staphylococcal impetiginisation, treated with flucloxacillin.
Eczema herpeticum features punched-out umbilicated vesicles, not golden honey-coloured crusts.
Fungal infection does not present with golden crusting and Staph aureus.
Emollients alone cannot clear acute pyogenic staphylococcal infection.
items.kp: Honey-coloured crusting on eczema indicates secondary staphylococcal infection; treat with flucloxacillin.
items.source: NICE guideline CG57: Atopic eczema in under 12s: diagnosis and management

x.key: Golden crusting indicates staphylococcal impetiginisation requiring flucloxacillin.

others.C: Fungus does not cause golden crusts.
others.D: Emollients alone fail to treat bacterial infection.

x.pearl: Topical fusidic acid must be restricted to strict short courses (<14 days) to prevent widespread staphylococcal resistance.
x.clues: Eczema child, honey-coloured crusting, Staph aureus on swab.
x.ddx: Eczema herpeticum, streptococcal impetigo, acute contact dermatitis.
x.mech: Fibronectin exposure in excoriated atopic skin provides binding ligands for Staphylococcus aureus adhesins.
x.lo: Recognise and manage secondarily impetiginised atopic eczema.
x.rev: Honey-coloured crusts signify secondary staphylococcal infection in eczema, requiring flucloxacillin.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman with severe atopic eczema requires frequent courses of potent topical steroids on her eyelids and neck, leading to cutaneous atrophy and striae. Which topical non-steroidal immunomodulator is licensed and recommended as a steroid-sparing agent for delicate sites?
items.exp: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.03% and 0.1% ointment, and pimecrolimus cream) are licensed second-line treatments for atopic eczema. Because they do not inhibit collagen synthesis, they do not cause skin atrophy, telangiectasia or striae, making them ideal steroid-sparing agents for the face, eyelids, and neck.
r: Correct: Topical tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor that spares steroid atrophy on the face and neck.
Fluorouracil is a cytotoxic antimetabolite for actinic keratoses and basal cell carcinoma.
Imiquimod is an immune response modifier for warts and superficial BCC.
Podophyllotoxin is an antimitotic for anogenital warts.
items.kp: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) provide steroid-sparing therapy without causing cutaneous atrophy.
items.source: NICE guideline CG57 / Technology Appraisal TA82: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus for atopic eczema

x.key: Topical tacrolimus is a non-steroidal calcineurin inhibitor that avoids skin atrophy.

others.B: Fluorouracil is cytotoxic for actinic keratosis.
others.C: Imiquimod is for warts and BCC.

x.pearl: Patients should be warned that a transient burning or stinging sensation is common during the first few days of tacrolimus application.
x.clues: Steroid atrophy on eyelids and neck, requiring non-steroidal topical agent.
x.ddx: Topical steroid withdrawal, perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis.
x.mech: Inhibits calcineurin phosphatase, preventing dephosphorylation of NFAT and blocking IL-2 transcription in T-lymphocytes.
x.lo: Identify topical calcineurin inhibitors as steroid-sparing agents in atopic eczema.
x.rev: Topical tacrolimus is an effective steroid-sparing agent that avoids cutaneous atrophy.

next.text: Review NICE TA82 on calcineurin inhibitors.
